speechtext:
1.	No, it is not the intention to erect a roundhouse at Sussex. There is only one engine that stands there over night, and a suitable building to house this engine will be built during this summer.

1. Is the government aware of the condition of affairs indicated by the following extract from the report of ,the commission appointed to inquire into thfe Martineau defalcation :-
' Although not strictly within the terms of the commission, the commissioners cannot refrain from bringing to the notice of the government the danger from fire to the records in the upper 147
part of the Eastern Block, owing to the proximity of the steam-pipes to the woodwork in the corridor leading to the Indian Department. They think this calls for Immediate attention. The charred condition of the floor touching the pipes shows that a conflagration is imminent, and measures should be taken to avert it. The lack of provision against fire also applies to the attic of the Langevin Block, where the records of the surveys under the control of the Department of the Interior are stored. These records are exceedingly valuable, as they represent the results of very large outlays of public money, and cannot be duplicated.'
2.	Is it the intention to guard against such a contingency ?
3.	Are the Are appliances in the various public buildings ever tested to see if they are in working order ?

1.	The steam heating pipes in attic of eastern block run in brick trenches covered by wooden traps which are lined with tin. At the place referred to the tin was stripped off the hoards which were discoloured, but there is no danger as there is no authentic instance known of a steam-pipe setting fire to wood. In the attic of the Langevin block the floors are fireproof and the roof of iron-and in the attic and roof there are four hydrants connected with the electric fire pump and two connected with the city pressure.
2.	The matter will receive the attention of the department.. The government contemplate the erection of a special building for the storage of records.
3.	Yes. The electric pumps are examined and tested every three or four days and the hydrants and, chemical fire extinguishers throughout the buildings are in charge of the Dominion police and are kept in order and tested regularly by the force.

House again in Committee on Bill (No. 181) to amend the Patent Act.-The Minister of Agriculture.
On section 7, subsection a,

I do not know whether the point which I brought up in the absence of the minister has been considered. The case is something like this. A gentleman invented a certain apparatus. One of his workmen who had assisted in its manufacture left his employ and made some of the machines, and they were in use while the inventor's application for his patent was before the department. I understand that under the law at present there is nothing to prevent the use of these machines, and the patentee cannot interfere.

This Bill makes no change in that respect,



and I do not quite see how it would be possible for us to take the matter up. After the application is put in and until the patent issues, the patent is not valid and there is nothing to prevent the use of the article. If at the time of the application the machine was in use, the application would have to be rejected; but I do not know how we could protect a patentee in a case in which the article was manufactured and used while the application was pending.
I would like the minister to look into the case. I think it was before the department a month or six -weeks ago.

The only cases that come before the department is where a workman who has also made a machine applies for the patent as well as the inventor. There is then a conflict between the two which has to be decided by reference to arbitration.
But how will the department proceed to stop the other man from using the machine ?

That would be a question for the law courts.
On section 9,
The validity of any extension heretofore granted or assumed to be granted under section 37 of the said Act, of the period of two years limited by that section, or by that section as heretofore amended, for the commencement of the construction or manufacture of a patented invention, or of the period of twelve months thereby limited for the importation of the patented invention, shall not be open to impeachment, because-
(a.) such extension was so granted or assumed to be granted by the deputy commissioner of patents, or, as acting deputy commissioner of patents, by a person performing the duties of deputy Minister of Agriculture under the provisions of the Civil Service Act in that behalf, instead of by the commissioner of patents ; or because
(b.) in the case of the invention to which such extension relates, there had been granted or assumed to be granted a previous extension or previous extensions of the period of two years or the period of twelve months, as the case may he, so limited.

I move that after the word 'impeachment,' in the thirtieth line, the following he added: * Nor shall the patent of any invention in respect of which such extension has been granted be deemed to have elapsed or expired.'
Several of these artificial light patents have expired, will any of them be re-established by this Bill ?

This Bill will not reinstate any patent whose term has expired. The only patents to he affected by this are those which had complied with the law, as interpreted by the Hon. Mr. FISHER.
department, but which interpretation was set aside by the Supreme Court in December last in the case of Power vs. Griffin. That court decided three main points ; first, that being ready to manufacture was not sufficient, as it had been held to be by the department, to fulfil the requirements of the manufacturing clause ; second, that the extension of time by the deputy or acting deputy was not valid and that only the minister could make that extension ; third, that not more than one extension could he given. Under this reading of the law, there is a considerable number of patents which have not fulfilled those requirements, although they had fulfilled the requirements as formerly held by that department. This Bill would reinstate the patents which had thus expired and lapsed. Besides the Bill goes into the point of the existence in Canada being dependent on the existence of the same patent in a foreign country, and relieves the patentees in this country from-the necessity of renewing their patents in foreign countries. In consequence of the change in section 9, it will be necessary to make corresponding amendments in sections 10 and 14. I would therefore move that after the words ' be impeached ' in section 10, the following words be added :	' Nor shall such patent
be deemed to have lapsed or expired.' I also move that in the subsection 2 of section 10, after the word ' section ' the following be inserted :	' Or which by reason of the
provisions of this subsection is to he deemed not to have lapsed or expired.'

Motion agreed to.
Mr. BUkDEN (Halifax). These amendments I suppose are simply in line with what has been done in section 9 ? It is a little difficult to follow the effect of amendments made in this way.

Yes, the insertion of these words is simply to carry out what has been done in section 9. Section 14 should also he amended by the addition of the following words after the word 'Act' :	'Or which, by reason of any
such provision is to be deemed not to have lapsed or expired.' Then, there is an omission in tlm printing which makes it necessary to add, after the word ' sell ' the words ' the same.' Then, I wish to add to section 14 :
And in case any person has contracted with the owner of the patent for the right to manufacture, use, or sell such patent in Canada, such contract, which shall be deemed to have remained in full force and effect, notwithstanding that the patent may have become void as aforesaid.
This will have the effect of validating the contracts. As we are reinstating the patents, it seems only fair that we should validate the contracts also.
The object ef this section is entirely different from this amendment.
I think not The object of the section is to protect acquired rights, and the idea of this is that contracts in connection with the patent rights are rights and should remain in force.

But the scope of section 14 is to provide that persons who have begun to manufacture while the patents were actually void may continue to manufacture notwithstanding the enactment of the Bill. The proposed amendment deals with rather the converse of that, namely that the revival of the patent shall he accompanied by the continuance of any contract between the owner of the patent and any third person. I understand the purpose, but it seems a little remote from the purpose of section 14. I would suggest that it would be a little more in conformity with the scope of the Act to amend some previous section or add a subsection.

I see the point made by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Borden, Halifax) and think there is a good deal of force in what he says. In this matter I took the advice of the Department of Justice and they seemed to think that this clause would be sufficient. I would not object to inserting it before clause 14. or we could contrive a clause. Perhaps it would be better to leave it as it is here drawn by the law officers. I would move that this clause be added to section 14.

Do the concluding words of section 14 as it stands at present, cover everything the minister intends :
Any person who has, between the time whvn such' patent became void or when the ground for such impeachment arose, and the time of the passing of this Act, commenced to manufacture, use or sell in Canada the invention covered by such patent, may continue to manufacture, use or sell in as full and ample a measure as if this Act had not been passed.

The expression ' inveution ' in the interpretation clause of the Patent Act is defined to mean ' any new and useful art, machine, manufacture or composition of matter, or any new and useful improvement in any art, machine, manufacture or composition of matter.' So the word ' invention ' is intended to cover anything that is patentable.
Have you a provision in this Act that it should be construed as one with the Patent Act ?
This is an amendment to the Patent Act, it is not a new Act.

I do not remember whether there is any provision in the Interpretation Act that amendments shall he always regarded and construed ns one with the general Act. We want to make that definition apply to this Act.

The Minister of Justice says that amendments to any Act come under the interpretation clauses of the Act.
Section, as amended, agreed to.
Bill reported.

I would like the Bill to stand a day or two for the third reading. Some suggestions have been made to me with regard to amendments which I hardly think are necessary, because I think they are already covered by the terms of the Bill. But I would like to communicate with the gentlemen who have made these suggestions and indicate to them what my own opinion is with regard to it. and ascertain whether they have anything further to suggest.
Certainly.
It might he well to have it reprinted now before reading it the third time.
I think I can arrange that.

Bill (No. 17S) respecting the encouragement of the construction of dry-docks, read the second time, and House went into committee thereon.
On section 1.
-The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Hon. W. S. Fielding). The general features of this Bill were discussed at an earlier stage. There are a couple of new provisions necessary to carry out the arrangement which is contemplated. We have provided in the general clauses which we discussed in committee, for the increase of the amount of subsidy, and I stated that provision would be made for a tariff of fees in these, dry docks, to be submitted to the government. If hon. gentlemen will give their attention to section 2 they will find we have Inserted a clause providing that no tolls or rates should be levied except those which have the approval of the government. There is a further clause that the company should be obliged to submit a statement of its affairs, showing the exact amount of money which it has realized from the issue of the various classes of stocks, and all the aids it has received from public bodies. The object is that if we are to be called upon to judge as to the fairness of the rates, we must know what amount of actual cash has been invested in the enterprise, so that we may fix such tolls as may yield a fair return on the cash actually invested in the project. These are the only clauses which have been added to the Bill since the matter was discussed in committee.
On section 1,

Has the government any policy on the question as to the establishment of dry-docks ? I see that there are, in this section, these words :
If any company or body corporate approved by the Governor in Council as having the ability to perform the work.
Is it understood to be the policy of the government, that, if a body of gentlemen come forward and show that they have the financial ability after another body of gentlemen have been assisted, they shall be equally helped, or is it going to be laid down as the policy of the government that no second dock shall be instituted or helped by the government, because, upon tlio help it receives will depend the commencement and completion of the work in its entirety, without some fixed rule being laid down as to the number of miles that must intervene between the dock already assisted and the one proposed to be built 7

There is no fixed rule as respects that point. 1 take it for granted that if a dock had been constructed in any locality and it was shown that it was not able to meet the demands of business, and another dock was proposed to be built, that would be a matter for consideration. As to the number of miles that should intervene, that point has never come before us and I think, as I suggested, that the matter will settle itself pretty well commercially. It is not likely that another body of men will desire to build another dock unless there is room for another dock in a commercial way.
Then are we to understand that no second dock will be assisted unless it has been shown that the dock that has been assisted has been inadequate for the requirements of business ?
I have already told my hon. friend (Mr. Bennett) that there is no fixed rule or policy of the government at all. Each case will have to be dealt with on its merits as it arises.

I understand the hon. minister to state that it is a condition precedent that it must first be shown that the government-assisted dock has been entirely unable to cope with the requirements of the trade.
The conditions precedent are the conditions laid down in the statute. I cannot by any words of mine lay down conditions.
But you can lay down the line of policy which the government intend to pursue ?

I do not think, this is a matter which calls for a more definite decision of policy than has Hon. Mr. FIELDING.
already been laid down. I think the matter will settle itself commercially. 1 do not think there is any danger of a company establishing another dock where there is one in a locality which is able to do the business.

I understand the hon. minister to say-of course ' Hansard ' will show whether he made the statement or not-that the government will not entertain any proposals for the assistance of a new dry-dock until it has been shown that the established dry-dock, in a certain locality and assisted by the government, has been unable to cope with the business. After that it would be quite in order on the eve of a general election to appeal to Midland, Owen Sound and other towns with the promise that a government supporter's return will result in the establishment of a dry-dock, and I am quite confident that I will be able to show that the hon. Minister of Finance made the statement that this would be one of the conditions under which such a proposition would be entertained.
If my hon. friend can get so much comfort out of my remarks as that, I would be sorry to deny them, but I think he will find that they will not bear the interpretation that he puts upon them.
I would like to ask the hon. Minister of Finance whether the government will have any say as to the charges which shall be made for the use of this dry-dock ?

Yes, it is proposed that the owners of the dock must charge according to a tariff which has been submitted to the government, because, when they are receiving this large amount of public aid we think they shall establish fair and reasonable rates.
Has the government any report as to the probable cost of this werk ?

I have not heard anything on the subject since the last discussion took place. The hon. Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Sutherland) is not in his place and I do not know whether he has anything on the subject or not. However, we will be able to ascertain later.

What is the meaning of the words ' on the cost of the work ? ' Surely it does not refer to repairs. The old dock is entering into the construction of this dock at Collingwood. The section says :
The Governor in Council may authorize the payment .... of a subsidy not exceeding three per cent per annum on the cost of the work.
Then, there is a qualifying clause at the end which says :
4:631

The cost on which it shall be calculated shall not be greater than the value of the work as estimated by the said minister.

These are not new words. These are words which have been in the Act for twenty years. The purpose I have no doubt is that while we may pay interest on the cost, we shall not pay a subsidy on an extravagant cost. They must submit an estimate and they must satisfy the minister that the cost is the bona fide cost, so that we shall only pay a subsidy in return for a bona fide expenditure.

While these words might have a certain interpretation if an absolutely new dock was being constructed the hon. Minister of Finance will, of course, recollect that in the resolution as passed and in this Bill as proposed the words include the completion of a dry-dock now in course of construction. In this dock at Collingwood, for example, a portion of a former dock constitutes an important part of the new dock. If you were building a completely new dock you could say what is to be the actual cost of the work. But, suppose you introduce into the question a portion of an old dock partly completed, such as there is at Collingwood, and which has not been built under the supervision of the Department of Public Works, a difficulty would be introduced, which you would have to consider.

A work having been completed might be useless for want of. repairs, and it might be said that the work is worth more because of the impairs. It is a question whether you would pay on the total value as it was then or merely on the cost of putting it into shape.

I do not quite follow the hon. gentleman's argument, but I hardly think the word ' new ' would properly express it because this paragraph is apparently contemplating new work and it would be a redundancy to put in the word ' new.' I think it would be safer to say that this -would only be calculated on the alluding to what you think might be the expenditure on an existing work.
speakername: The POSTMASTER GENERAL (Hon. Sir William Mulock).

speechtext: Suppose you have a dry-dock that might be valued" by the owners at $50,000 and you want to build a dock that will cost when completed $300.-000-a new company pays $50,000 for the old dock although they might not get value for more than $15,000. If you insert the word ' new ' it would prevent them getting any return on the money they had to pay for the old dock, and which would be an expenditure on their part just as much as if it were for a new work. I think we should pause before inserting that word.

There is also the danger that the cost of the land which might be a very considerable item could not be taken into account if you inserted that word. I can assure my hon. friends that there is no intention of subsidizing any old broken down enterprise.

The dry-dock at Collingwood was assisted by the town to the extent of $50,000 and the town got possession of it and made an absolute present of it to this company. In such a case assistance should be given only to the new work.

If the corporation of a town gave them some aid, that would certainly enter into the valuation for which they would receive a subsidy, but they could not earn a tariff of tolls on it. We have provided that they must make returns on all aids received from corporations and they cannot earn any money on that.
This company at Collingwood should have no claim on the government for the site or for any assistance that the town gave. *
I would not like to answer that off-hand.
But they should not.
The hon. gentleman need not be concerned about Col-

I think that to say that the dock at Collingwood is an old dock repaired, is hardly to make a fair statement. The information we have is that the dock at Collingwood is practically an entirely new dock. The only excuse for saying anything about the old dock is that there was an old dock in former years. It was a small affair, and I understand all that remains of the old dock is a hole in the ground and that that hole is not big enough for the purposes of the new dock. I understand that there is nothing of the old dock there to-day so that properly speaking it is a new dock that is to be built at Collingwood.
'Mr. LANCASTER. Might I suggest that in the 27th line of the section you insert the word ' new ' before the word ' work ? ' If the hon. Minister of Finance means to pay this subsidy only on a new work instead of on a work partly old and partly new this will make it clearer.

That is certainly the intention, and for the present I see no objection to the proposed amendment. We might reserve the third reading of the Bill lest we find that this amendment contains something that we do not intend, but I see no reason why the hon. gentleman's amendment should not be ac. cepted.

lingwood, because I made a statement at an. earlier stage of this debate and I received a letter since from the president of tiie company, Mr. John Long, in which he says that my reference to conditions at Coiiingwood were correct. I may repeat what I then said. I stated that it was true that they began with the hope that they would utilize some of the walls of the existing dock, but they found it impossible to make any use whatever of them, and instead of getting any benefit they had to go the extra expense of removing the walls so that all that was left was the hole in the ground. So far as Coiiingwood is concerned, there was practically no value to the company in the dock which they attempted to enlarge, and ultimately had to abandon.
That is not inconsistent with my statement that the company had to pay nothing for it.
I do not know anything as to how they acquired it.

They are in possession of the work which the town gave them for the benefit of the town and the country in the hope of getting government assistance. This company has expended nothing except to remove the old works as the Postmaster General states.
The POSTMASTER GENERAL Expended nothing on what ?
On the dock; excepting the removal of a portion of it which could not be utilized.
They are expending a much larger amount of money than the subsidy.
I know, but what I wish to guard against is the value of property being calculated before these new works are commenced.
I would like to ask the Minister of Finance whether this three per cent bonus applies as well to a floating dock as to a dry-dock.

The wording of the Act deals with dry-docks, and I think we have never had application for the construction of a floating dock. A case of that kind might have to be dealt with by special legislation. If there is a place where a floating dock is more suitable than a dry-dock, that might have to be considered.

There is a large company in the city of Vancouver who contemplate the building of a floating dock, and I doubt if they would be likely to go into the enterprise unless they were assured of the three per cent bonus from the Dominion government. As a matter of fact a floating dock is much preferable to a dry-dock.

I am inclined to think that a floating dock is a dry-dock, so that it would come under the operation of this dock. A dry-dock means a dock that is made dry so that you can repair a vessel, and I suppose a floating dock would answer the purpose of repairing vessels the same as a dry-dock. There would therefore be no difference in reality between a floating dock and a dock on land. The essence of the thing is that you should have a dock where you may repair ships, and whether afloat or ashore I think it would come under the spirit of the Act.
It is not a dry-dock when you fill it with water so that vessels may be floated into it.
The Bermuda dry-dock was taken out from England.
I understand there is an engineer from the Public Works Department superintending the construction of the dock at Coiiingwood.
It has been built under the general direction of the Department of Public Works, but whether they have a resident engineer there or not I would not like to answer.
I think the Postmaster General said on a previous occasion that the work was being done under the superintendence of an officer of the department.
The plans have to be approved by the department.
It is not necessary to have a resident engineer, but for their own satisfaction the department may have sent an engineer.
As the minister has assented to the insertion of the word ' new,' I think it covers all objections.

I am afraid that the insertion of that word would make it too restrictive. For instance, you could not pay for the land in the case of the St. .Tohn dry-dock, and my hon. friend (Mr. Lancaster) does not mean that. I think the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Haggart) can safely accept the assurance of the Postmaster General, who is familiar with Coiiingwood, that it is a new dock, and that there is no question of repairing an old one.
The insertion of the word ' new ' would certainly cover the cost of the land.
I am not sure that it would.

You might as well take our assurance as to ask us to take the assurance of the Postmaster General.

46S6
The one is a matter of law and the other is a matter of fact. We are able to form an opinion on a matter of fact, but when it comes to a matter of law we have to refer it to our legal adviser.
We are all agreed that there slfculd be some improvement in the clause in the direction intended, and if the insertion of the word ' new,' may not suit, we may perhaps get something else.

The Act in that respect is exactly as it has been for "twenty years, and, as none of these difficulties have ever arisen, I think hon. gentlemen rather magnify them, especially after all the conversations we have had with' reference to the Collingwood dock ; and I am afraid that if we amend the Bill to meet that case, we might put an obstruction in the way of the erection of docks elsewhere.

I had not in mind the Collingwood dock ; but it struck me that as the object of the Act is no doubt to encourage the construction of works which will be useful for the purpose, we are not to pay upon anything except what has been brought into existence by the people who are looking for a subsidy. As the clause reads now, if there was some work of value done before the new work, it could be strongly argued that the whole work, after its completion, would be entitled to a subsidy, although perhaps only 25 per cent of the work might be required to make it a complete work. In such a case, I do not think over 25 per cent of the work ought to get the subsidy. I think there should be a qualifying word of some kind inserted in the section.

The object which my friend has in view is commendable, but I am afraid that the word inserted there might possibly defeat itself. Let us dispose of the Bill in committee, and we will look into it and see if any change is needed later on.

Did I understand the hon. Postmaster General to say that he had received a communication from the president of the Collingwood Dry-dock Company in which that gentleman said that the old work had no value, or that there was nothing of it there to-day except the hole ?

I said I had received a letter from Mr. John Long, the president of the Collingwood company, stating that he had read the debate in ' Hansard ' and had read my statements in that debate, and that they were correct.
' Mr. CLARKE. I think the minister added something else.

No, nothing more than what I have said just now. When the matter was before the House on
a former occasion, I stated that I had visited Collingwood and had seen the condition of the work, and I described the extent of the new work, which practically made the whole thing a new work.
Then there was nothing left of the old outfit ?
There was nothing left but the hole of the smaller dock.
Were the walls wood or concrete ?
When I was there, there was only one wall partially built-the east wall of the new structure, and it was of stone. There was excavation going on in other directions.
The only part of the old dock to be taken into account is the hole ?
That is my information.

The dry-dock which formerly existed at Collingwood was not by any means an unimportant work. It -was capable of accommodating the Canadian Pacific Railway steamers, which are over 300 feet in length. I myself have seen them in that dock. It was also stated in the debate the other day by the hon. member for North Grey (Mr. Thomson) that it was a very fine dock. It must be quite clear that when this company took the old dock as a present from the town of Collingwood, it was a dock of considerable value, and if the walls were of stone, this new company have a very valuable asset. I assume that the government do not propose to pay on the material taken from the old dock which enters into the construction of the new dock, and of which this company have been made a present 1

Even if they did, it might not be such a monstrous thing as the hon. gentleman seems to suppose, if the dock as originally constructed received no subsidy. However, I do not think that is likely to arise in this case. Tliese.docks are sometimes given assistance from various quarters.
The town gave $50,000 of cash bonus to the company which failed.

I know that in the case of the Halifax dock the city gave a large sum, and yet the subsidy could be collected on the whole cost of the dock. I do not see anything wrong in that. It is by a combination of these various aids that people get the resources to build the docks. If the land for the Collingwood dock was a free gift from the town, it still formed a fair part of the cost of the dock. I do not think we should object to that.

The Department of Public Works should be able to supply all

the information required by the committee. Although Mr. Coste has been supervising this work, and has visited Collingwood time and again in connection with it, we are without a single bit of information in regard to what has been done.
That shows that the Department of Public Works are carefully looking after the work, and I do not think we should apologize for that.

There is no provision as to the use of the docks by United States ships. In the case of Halifax, under the contract with the Imperial government, which gave also some aid. it was provided that Her Majesty's ships should have the first use.

Mr.-CLARICE. But should we not have priority ?

that we need fear any difficulty on that score.

The hon. gentleman should provide that the company shall not do as the old company did, utilize the dock for the purpose of constructing vessels in it. In all seriousness, if there is anything in the statement made by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Hon. Mr. Prdfontaine) recently, that the government intend to establish the nucleus of a Canadian navy, there should be right reserved in the Bill for priority for repairs of government vessels whenever there is necessity.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext:
This Bill was passed in committee except section 12, which was reserved for consideration of suggestions made by the hon. member for East Middlesex (Mr. Gilmour). Whenever the animal is not thus infected but has been in contact *with or in dangerous proximity to diseased animals, the compensation, if any, shall be three-quarters of the value of the animal, but shall not exceed, in the case of grade animals, fifty dollars, or in the case of pure bred animals one hundred and fifty dollars. Provided that when it is clearly shown that the animal has been slaughtered<on insufficient grounds and that the slaughter was not in accordance with or justifiable under this Act, the owner shall be entitled to compensation in the full value of the animal so slaughtered.
