speechtext:
It seems to me that some words should be inserted here providing for the consent of the municipality
being first obtained. I question very much whether people, relying on this Act, might not get into serious difficulty if a municipality denied the right of the board under all circumstances to allow a railway to run on a highway in a city or town or incorporated village, or in fact any organized municipality. There might be some circumstances in which that would be absolutely necessary. I know the argument that is used, that when you charter a railway to go from one point to another point, and it is necessary to the purposes of the charter that the railway should pass over highways, the Dominion parliament has a primn facie right over the highways to that extent. But that is so only where it is absolutely necessary. There might be a hundred other ways of getting from the one point to the other point. I think we should be passing | dangerous and unsafe legislation in providing that if the board saw fit, it could compel the municipality to let a railway be constructed on a highway. If the railway com- * pany could carry out the object of its charter by expropriating land beside the highway, no matter at what cost, even if it should be necessary to tear down buildings, to do so, I do not think this parliament can give it power over the public highways, and I do not think we ought to authorize any board of commissioners to do anything that it seems to me we have not the power to do ourselves. The prima facie power over the highways is vested in the local legislature, and through it is given to the municipalities, and under the British North America Act this parliament cannot use a highway wantonly. As we have power to charter a railway, we have power to authorize it to go through everything that is necessary for the purposes of the undertaking, but only when it is absolutely necessary. If it is not necessary, I doubt the power of this parliament to pass that section; I think it would be ultra vires. I do not think we ought to undertake to give this board the power to let a railway run upon or across a public highway without the consent of the municipality. If the board went on and undertook to compel the municipality to let the railw'ay run on its highway, and if the municipality fought against the order of the board, I am of opinion that the clause would be held to be ultra vires, and I do not think we should pass it.

I presume that all the works which are declared to be for the general advantage of Canada will be works over which the commissioners to be appointed under this Bill will have jurisdiction ? Session after session we are declaring enterprises to be for the general advantage of Canada, which are practically one-horse tramways; and if this section remains as it is, these commissioners will have the power to compel municipalities to admit such lines, whether they desire to

do so or not. Surely our great municipalities, like Toronto, Montreal, Hamilton and others, have some rights that ought to he taken into consideration; and if they set their faces against lines coming in which they do not want, we should not give the : commissioners power to compel them to give entrance to such lines. In the case of undertakings connecting one province with another, I can understand that no municipality should have the right to prevent their going through ; but in the case of purely local enterprises, I think that the municipalities should have the right of compelling such enterprises to first obtain their consent.

I am afraid that those gentlemen who express the decided opinion that this law is ultra vires the Parliament of Canada will find it somewhat difficult to establish their proposition. The law has been on the statute-book ever since the parliament of Canada was organized, and I think, a similar provision was contained in the Railway Act of the two provinces of Upper and Lower Canada; and I have not yet heard-and I think it would be difficult to show-that in any single instance it was ever contended before any court that the parliament of Canada has not the power to legislate in these terms. The matter suggested by the hon. member for Toronto. (Mr. Clarke) is worthy of consideration, but he must bear in mind that there must be some kind of authority to determine whether or not any public highway may be used by a railway. You cannot leave it in the hands of a municipality, to definitely determine that principle. When the parliament of Canada gives a charter to a corporation, under which the corporation has the right to go through a town, you cannot leave it to the municipality to say whether the charter power shall be exercised or not. You must leave it to some independent tribunal. Otherwise the municipal authorities might refuse to allow this power to be exercised, greatly to the public disadvantage. They might hold up a corporation and impose unreasonable exactions, and you would have no authority to pronounce upon the fairness or justice of the municipal demands. It has always been admitted by the parliament of Canada down to the present moment that such a power should reside in the Railway Committee of the Privy Council. In all its decisions, the tendency of the Railway Committee has been to yield to the wishes of the municipal corporations. I know of no instance in which a different course has been pursued, and the result has been that, witli this power in the hands of an independent tribunal, the municipal authorities have always been reasonable and willing to allow a thing to be done where it was unavoidable and where it would be for the general
convenience. It is necessary often for the convenience of the public that railway stations be located in the centre of a city so as to be easily accessible for business and other purposes. There is not likely to be any serious controversy under this Bill any more than under the law as it exists, and therefore I cannot see that it w'ould be well to repeal the law or change it materially. Experience has shown that no danger has arisen and no public injury has been done, or inconvenience suffered, and we may infer that the experience of the last forty years is likely to continue.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: There is a good deal of force in the argument of the hon. minister as regards the experience of municipalities, but a new condition of things has arisen during the past two or three years. Applications are made every session to this parliament for the incorporation of companies declared to be for the general advantage of Canada, but which are purely provincial. The introduction of electricity has made a marked difference in the situation. Enterprises are being promoted to connect city with city, and these enterprises, if sanctioned by the parliament of Canada, and declared to be for the general advantage of Canada, will come under the authority of this commission. They are not, in the strict sense of the term, works for the general advantage of Canada, but simply for the benefit of some small section of one of the provinces. Regulations have been passed by the legislatures of some of the provinces dealing with such matters, and I think that the direction and control of such purely provincial enterprises should be left With the provinces and not be taken by the Dominion. In the case of purely provincial lines, the right of a municipality to prevent any such line coming into it, without its consent, should be respected. The hon. minister has declared what is well known, that the municipalities have been reasonable in the past and have obtained justice from the Privy Council. There is no reason to assume that they will be otherwise in the future or demand unreasonable conditions from any enterprise within municipal bounds. But by the clause as amended
It is not different from the present law.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Now, a different condition of things has arisen
It is not due to this amendment.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: No, it is due to the application of electricity to railways and the granting of charters by this parliament to enterprises which it declares to be for the general benefit of Canada, tout which are

JUjSTE 15, 1903
purely local in tlieir character. And this power to give a railway company the right to run along a highway should not be exercised unless the enterprise is inter-provincial in its character.

The argument which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clarke) has addressed to the committee is inapplicable to the present Bill, but it would be applicable if the measure before the committee were to incorporate an electric tramway and declare it a work for the general benefit of Canada.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I asked the hon. minister if works and enterprises declared to be for the general advantage of Canada came under the purview of this commission, and he said they did. I am drawing his attention to the fact that we in this parliament are giving charters almost every day to railway companies that only intend to join one municipality with another, and declaring them to be works for the general advantage of Canada.- In view of this and of the new conditions created by the changes .in electric traction, I ask the hon. minister if he does not think that the municipalities ought to have their rights reserved to them ? The Railway Committee of the Privy Council, as I understand it, has hitherto dealt with steam railways only. But a new order of things is being created because of the legislation sought to be obtained from this parliament. If this clause is permitted to go as the hon. minister has amended it, whatever rights the municipalities enjoy to keep out lines of electric cars that they do not wish to have running along their highways, will be taken away. I think that is a serious matter that I am drawing the hon. minister's attention to, and the attention of the committee at large, to the subject, in the hope that something will be done to afford protection to the municipalities.

And I am drawing the hon. gentleman's (Mr. Clarke) attention to the fact that we are not discussing and cannot be supposed to discuss under this Bill, conditions which are special and exceptional such as the hon. gentleman refers to. It is open to the hon. gentleman if he desires, to annex a condition to the granting of every charter of an electric railway, whether it is declared to be a work for the general advantage of Canada or not-or to ask parliament to annex it-that these rights shall not be exercised through any city or town without the consent of the municipality. They would then be under the necessity of going to the municipality for any such power. But how does the bon. gentleman propose to amend this section ? He says, that as I have amended it, it causes a difficulty. He is in error in that respect. If he were a lawyer, he would
know that the verbal changes made in this clause from the words of the existing law do not create a new condition such as he says-they do .not alter the tenor or spirit of the law at all. The old section says that so and so shall not be done unless so and so, and this says that 'it may be done if so and so. There is no difference, as a matter of fact, as any lawyer would say if he were to express his opinion on it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: When this parliament declares a work to be a work for the general advantage of Canada, it gives to the company carrying out that work certain powers. This is the time to make an amendment to the law, because the changes in regard to electricity as a motive power create a new order of things for which the law should provide.
What amendment would the hon. gentleman propose ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: If I hacf the legal ability of the hon. minister-he has been good enough to remind me that I am not a lawyer-I could draft a clause. And if he will allow this section to stand I will see about >a clause being drafted.
The hon. gentleman has started a legal question, which he does not understand, I am sorry to say, and if be cannot propose an amendment
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I will he glad to submit an amendment if the hon. gentleman will allow the clause to stand.
This is a provision of great Importance, and I think that any tampering with it might lead to great misfortune.
It is tampered with now.

As has been stated by the hon. minister the clause as now proposed is exactly the same in effect as the old clause. It does seem to me that it should be our object to retain every section of the old Act unless some good reason is advanced for changing it. No good reason could be given for changing this clause. If the amendment were passed which is suggested by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clarke), I can see how small towns and municipalities' might be put in a position where they could tie up great railway enterprises. Suppose a railway runs for five hundred miles, then in the course of the construction it comes to a Village or small municipality which says. 'We will not permit you to cross our street.' And that street might be the only place where it could cross. Under the present law, before they can run along a street or cross a street they must get the sanction of the board. It seems to nie that this is a sufficient safeguard. We are putting large powers in the hands of that board, necessarily, and we must as-

sume that they will exercise those powers wisely as each case arises. I would therefore urge that there should be no change in this section.

The proposition which my hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Clarke) puts, as I understand it is this : Suppose a line runs from some town to the suburbs of a city and there connects with the city system of electric tramways, they would then have the right to run over the streets of the city. That, I take to be my hon. friend's contention. But as I understand the law, they could not do anything of the kind until they had received the sanction of the commission and of the civic authorities.
There is more than that in it. Under the general provisions of the law, an electric road must have the authority of the municipality to put up its poles.

Take the case of one of these roads spoken of by my hon. friend from AVest Toronto (Mr. Clarke), it receives a charter and' make a bargain with the municipality as to what streets it may run on. X am not talking now about crossing streets. This is even more dangerous; they can run along the street according to the Act.
Have they any different power from what they have had for forty years V
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
The danger is greater because, as my hon. friend has stated, the conditions are changed. AVhen this law was passed there were no electric railways, and railways did not run on one street where they run on a hundred to-day. I have no great regard for a law merely because it has been for many years in force, if it is not a law that applies to the conditions that actually exist. Here, let us say, is a concern with a charter from the Dominion parliament, and with the power under certain conditions, not merely to run across the street but to run along it, to use the highway for its right of way. Now, let me point out to the hon. member for Annapolis (Mr. Wade) that, even though It is arguable that this section as amended means the same thing as the old section, for some strange reason the phraseology is changed and changed in favour of the very view that my hon. friend from West Toronto and I are opposing. Now the sectioh under the old Act starts out :
The railway shall not he carried along an existing highway, but shall merely cross the same in the line of the railway.
Prima facie it shall not be carried along the highway but it shall cross it. Now how did they draw this section ? This section makes no distinction between crossing and going along. The draughtsmen of the old section, when they did not Mr. WADE.
have trouble with numerous electric roads wanting to cross highways, even then I saw a great distinction between a railway running across it. The legislature who passed that Act said :
Shall not be carried along an existing highway but shall merely cross the same in the line of the railway, unless leave therefor has been obtained from the Railway Committee, and no obstruction of such highway with the works shall he made without turning the highway so as to leave an open and good passage for carriages and on completion of the works, replacing the highway ; and every company which violates the provisions of this section shall incur a penalty of not less than $40.
I do not find that penalty carried out in the Bill which is now before us. Now, taking the section before us, the railway may be carried along or across an existing highway. As the minister drew this Bill which is before us, and which until a few minutes ago we supposed was to become law, it was not that way, it was that the railway shall not be carried along or upon. But for some reason, since this Act "was printed, we are surprised to-nlgbt to find that be is going to amend and puts the presumption the other way, the railway may be carried upon or along upon leave therefor obtained from the board.
The only difference is between tweedledum and tweedledee.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
Then why did the minister make it tweedledee when he had it tweedledum ? AVhy did he draw this section a second time and surprise the House with a new section, if it Is so unimportant? I think the section is different. If there are decisions and judicial rules that have operated before the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council under that old section, I can well understand where cases would arise where the same rule would not apply under this section. Prima facie, under the other section the railway could not be carried along or upon the highway. AVith all due deference to the minister's saying that there is no sense in contending this is ultra vires, I am still of the opinion that it is. The British North America Act has given the fullest power over highways for all general purposes to the municipalities through the provincial legislatures. As I have already said, I admit that in carrying out a work that the Dominion parliament has power to carry out, if it is necessary in order to carry a railway from one place to another to cross a highway, then parliament would have power to force its way through. But can there be a case where the Dominion parliament can say that it is absolutely necessary to run along a highway. There is land each side of a highway. True, it may lie expensive. I am satisfied that my suspicions are correct, and that it is because it is going to lie cheaper for a railway to go on tlie highway, if the board can be induced

to say that it may go there; the company, may pay a little money to the municipality, for paving or grading up the street a little, and then obstruct the highway for all time. Any large steam railway could run along! the highway here if the board gave permission. Now, suppose the city of Toronto or the city of St. Catharines gives a charter, and have passed a by-law giving power to; an electric railway to pass along a highway on certain terms only, and a steam railway wants to connect also on the highway. Suppose one of these lines is within the jurisdiction of this commission, this commission has power to force them to connect by this power it has of allowing a steam railway to run upon that same highway. The roads were not laid out for railway rights of way, they were laid out for highways In the ordinary sense of the word; and I still say that unless it is absolutely necessary to run along that highway this section would be ultra vires, if properly contested. This provision attempts to repeal the British North America Act in so far as it allows them to run along the highway, because I cannot conceive that it is absolutely necessary for any railway to run along the highway. There is land each side of the highway, otherwise there would not be a highway there, and that land can be used for the purposes of the railway and can be expropriated. Of course it will cost the railway some damages, and the object of this section is that when a company finds that it cannot build its road as cheaply as it thought it could be built without using the highway, the railway commission is to have power to allow them to use the streets of the city, town or village. . This is an authority that ought not to be delegated to them without the consent of the municipality, and we have not the right to delegate it to them under the British North America Act. That is for the provincial legislature.
The MINISTER OP RAILWAYS AND eANALS. I do not think there is the slightest foundation for the opinion which' the hon. gentleman has expressed. I am sure, from the conversations that took place in the Railway Committee of the Privy Council since I have had the honour of being a member of that board, that if it had been possible to raise a contention of that kind it would have been raised in several instances. The hon. gentleman says that he does not understand why the language of this clause was changed from the affirmative to the negative form. I will tell the hon. gentleman why. It was for the sake of harmonious and consistent legislation. We have passed in section 118 of the new Bill clause (k) 'make or construct in, upon, across, under or over any railway, tramway, river, stream, water-course, canal or highway.' and so on. Now that power is identical with the power we conferred upon the railway company in the existing Act, when it was passed many years ago. You will 148
find it in section 90 of the present railway law, which provides :
The company may, subject to the provisions of this Act. and of the special Act contained-
Do certain things and among, the rest:
Make, or construct in, upon, across, under, or near any .... highway.
And so on. What sense is there in giving to the railway company the power, of course, subject to the condition that the railway commission must approve, and then go on and say that the railway shall not be carried along the highway unless local approval has been obtained ? You have already said the company shall have that power. My hon. friend from East Northumberland (Mr. Cochrane) shakes his head.
I did not understand the hon. minister to read it in that way.

Section 90 of the present Railway Act says that the company may, subject to the provisions of this Act do the following things, among others :
Make, or construct in, upon, across, under cr near any railway, canal, river, stream or highway.	"
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: May the road be placed along the highway without the consent of the municipality ?
Yes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I am sure the hon. gentleman will see that this is a very serious question. I listened a moment ago when he said that the question had never been raised in all his experience
I said that the contention which was made here to-night that this power was ultra vires of this parliament had never been raised to my knowledge.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The hon. gentleman will see that this is an extraordinary power which can be used for the purpose of securing a right of way. I know nothing more serious than a railway constructed along the highway. I was going to say hundreds of accidents, but I will be safe in saving that the number reaches well up towards the hundreds, that I have known to occur as the result of a railway running alongside of a highway. Women and children may be driving alone, the horse becomes uncontrollable and a serious accident occurs. I do not say that in all cases! there should be no departure from the rule that a railway should not go along the highway, but if it can possibly be avoided it should be avoided.

I will accept the suggestion or proposition of the hon. minister, and I will undertake to try to have a clause



provided to be added which will meet the case that I am referring to. It is very difficult for a layman to express himself sometimes in order to convey to legal minds his exact idea. I asked the hon. minister if [DOT] enterprises and undertakings that were declared to be for the general advantage of Canada were to come under the purview of these railway commissioners and his answer was, yes. We are chartering tram car lines to run from one town to another in this province and they are declared to be works for the general advantage of Canada. We have these tram carlines surrounding cities and connecting with trunk lines. The conditions that are being created by this Bill are entirely different from those which have existed during the past forty or fifty years or since the Railway Act has been in operation. There is a new condition of things in existence, and I say that it is an intolerable outrage that these tram car railways shall be given permission to go into the city of Hamilton, or Toronto, or Montreal without the consent of the municipality. It is entirely unfair to the municipalities. Take the case of the city of Toronto, for instance: We have as complete a tram car system as can be found in any city in America. That system is operated by one company. The right to operate that surface line belongs to the city. The city has given that franchise for a number of years to a company. If the citizens of Toronto desire a more extended tram car service they are the best judges as to where these tram cars should come in and under what conditions, and they can acquire for them running rights over existing lines running through the streets of Toronto. But why should power be taken away from the municipalities to keep' these roads out if they desire to do so ? They are the best judges. These tram car lines that are getting incorporation from this parliament are not gift enterprises. They are not being established by philanthropists to put money into people's pockets. Surely the municipalities have some rights in the matter. They ought to have some opportunity of saying when and where these roads should come in and under what conditions. This parliament is surely not in the helpless condition that the hon. minister described it to be in, that it cannot make such an amendment to section 184 as will give the municipalities the right to state conditions under which a tram car line may come in, and not leave the matter entirely under the control of this board of commissioners. I am sure the hon. minister must understand the objection I am trying to present to this permission being given, in view of the new order of things which has been created by the introduction of electricity during the last four or five years.

If the hon. gentleman will turn his attention to sections 192 and 193 he will see that the very thing in regard to which he is now objecting is amply provided for. It provides that the company shall not place any lines, wires or p'oles on the streets until they have first obtained the consent of the board and then until they have obtained the consent of the municipality.
What board ?
Subsection ' f ' of section 193 says that the work of the company upon the highway shall be subject to the supervision of the municipality.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Clarke) is not wanting in apprehension, and yet I am surprised to hear him say that when a general law is passed for the management, control and regulation of railways, the proper exercise of these powers is impossible because there are some tramways which are brought within the control of this commission and which are declared to be works for the general advantage of Canada. My hon. friend talks about taking power away from the municipalities. Who is taking power away from the municipalities, if it is a proper power for the municipalities to exercise ? My hon. friend is taking it away from the municipalities-
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: No.

Yes, he is; he is taking it away from the municipalities in the Bills which are passed for the purpose of incorporating these railways, without any conditions saying that they shall not enter upon the streets of any municipality until they obtain the consent of the municipality for that purpost. Instead of destroying or mutilating this Bill, all he has to do is to put that clause in a special Act, and the special Act will govern, and until they have complied with the conditions that are to be found in that special Act they do not come within the general provisions of this Railway Act. That is a complete answer to the difficulty the hon. gentleman presents.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: No.
I say as a lawyer that is is.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: That is new doctrine.
New doctrine ; is it ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Yes, the government are responsible.
Another Daniel come to judgment.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I may be lacking in legal knowledge, but 1 think that primarily the responsibility for legislation o'f this kind rests on the hon. gentleman who occupies the distinguished position of Minister of Railways and Canals. If any injustice is being done to municipalities, the responsibility for that injustice must be shared by the minister with other members of this House when he allows tram car outfits run by electricity to be declared to be works for the general advantage of Canada. The hon. gentleman sits in the Railway Committee and he cannot be blind to the attempts that are frequently made with the object of destroying municipal rights. I enter my protest as a member of this House against legislation of this class that is being enacted here from year to year. The minister will see that the end is not yet, and that this question is bound to come before the House sooner or later. I am sure that the minister has sufficient legal knowledge, if he desired to exercise it, to enable him to add a subclause to this section which would meet the cases that we are presenting to him and which would protect the municipalities in the rights which they have enjoyed up to the present time. If the minister will give me permission I will try to get a lawyer to prepare a subclause that will meet the case, if he allows this section to stand.

Let the section stand.
Section allowed to stand.
On section 185,
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I wish to draw the attention of the minister to the words of this clause which say that the top of the rail may protrude an inch over the level of the surrounding street. Would not that be a serious impediment to traffic.

In all the by-laws that I have seen drawn, allowing these tramways or electric roads to run, they have always been compelled to put the top of the rail flush with the street, and the street is usually macadamized or paved up to the rail on both sides. Serious accidents will happen, runaways be caused and vehicles broken, if you allow the rail to obtrude in this way. It is admitted to be a most dangerous thing to allow the rail to rise above the level of the street. This difficulty arises because this House of Commons to-night is undertaking to do the work which should be done by the municipal councils throughout the country.

It is the experience of gentlemen who live in cities, that there is very great danger to horses and vehicles from allowing the rails to protrude above the level of the street. I have seen the tram car tracks laid down in the leading cities of the old country, and they are so level that you cannot detect any move-1484
ment of the wheels of your vehicle when you are crossing them. Why should we not make provision here that they should be level with the pavement ? It will not cost any more, and it will save a great deal of trouble. I am not an engineer, but I would suggest to the minister that it would be no hardship if we provided that the rails should be flush with the contiguous surface of the street.
We are simply retaining the latfr as it is now and always has been.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Why should that be an argument. That's a regular Tory doctrine and has been exploded long ago. If the law has allowed a dangerous thing in the past the law should be amended. That is ah there is to it. The minister knows as well as any farmer that it is very dangerous to allow these rails to protrude above the level of the roadway. If the rail is one inch above the roadway the wheels are likely to sink an inch below, and then you have two inches to get over, which is a serious obstacle. I do not care if the law has been so for generations, it should be rectified if it is not proper legislation. What might be right twenty years ago may be all wrong now.

You cannot always have the track just on the dead level with the highway. I am not talking about tramways, I am talking about railways, and we are legislating here for every railway in the Dominion. You make them liable to a penalty of I think $5,000, and if it is impossible to have the rail on a dead level, are you going to fine them, or are you goiug to wipe out the penalty altogether. That might be all right in reference to the streets of Toronto and some of the wealthy cities whose roadways are in fine condition, but you cannot make a law as stringent as that to apply to every railway crossing in Canada, because it is impossible to do it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Nearly all the by-laws of all the municipalities in Ontario compel the rail to be on the level, and they enforce those by-laws.	.
They cannot enforce that.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The by-law says that if the rail is not placed in that way the work will be done at the expense of the town engineer and the town collects the cost from the railway. If we did not interfere with the rights of the municipalities here the thing could be worked out all right, and that very fact proves that we should not undertake such legislation without the consent of the municipality.

I think it is very important that the roadway should be level with the track, especially in winter time. Our

teams, loaded with lumber, have often got stuck on the rails owing to the track being higher than the roadway. That is something that has happened in my observation several times. It is more dangerous to have the rails above than below the level. I think it would be in the interest of the railway company as well as of the public to have the roadway as high as the rails, if not higher.
What locality does the hon. gentleman refer to ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The township of Oso, in the county of Frontenac.

I do not think a stronger argument could be urged in favour of a modification of this clause than that presented by the hon. member for Addington (Mr. Avery). Why not provide that when the work is completed the top rail shall sink an inch below the highway ? Why allow the rail to obtrude an inch above the highway ? The damage is done by being above, not below.
If the rail is below the level, the wheels of wagons will be liable to get twisted.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
It is not unreasonable to expect the company to keep their rails level with the ground on either side. It is not safe to give them two inches of margin, because if they have it, they will take it. I would respectfully suggest to the minister that that clause ought to be modified in some way to make it more acceptable to the municipalities than it is as it stands now.
Mr. JOHNSTON [DOT](Cardwell). I may add that I have time and again seen teams stuck at crossings on country roads, and neighbouring teams have had to be got to help to pull them off. I myself got stuck at a railway crossing with a load of saw-logs, and I had to get another team to help to pull it off. As the law allows the rails to be an inch above the level, if a man's sleigh got stuck on it. the company could come along and smash it and he would have no remedy against them. I think in all country places the railway company should be compelled to keep their rails as low as the planks. That would save a great deal of trouble to the farmers and their teams. Then you often see a crossing where the railway does not cross the highway at right angles, but diagonally. Where it crosses at right angles, there is not so much difficulty with wheels, but where it crosses diagonally, a heavily loaded wagon or a sharp-tired buggy is liable to break an axle, hy running along the rail. If the rails were below the level, that could not happen.

If the minister has no objection to making this change, it would be a great benefit to the country at large. Last winter I had a dozen teams get stuck Mr. AVERY.
on the railway simply because the rails were higher than the roadway. To keep the rails down to the level or below the level of the roadway would not hurt the running of the railway, and it would keep the sleighs off the rails. It is very dangerous at present to cross with a heavy load if you have not an extra team to pull you off. The objection is not so great in summer as in winter, because a wheel will go over where a sleigh will not. I think the change proposed would be for the benefit of the railway company as well as the public.

I am willing to have the section stand for further consideration.
Section allowed to stand.
On section 188,
The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS moved that the section be so amended as to read as follows
The highway at any overhead railway crossing shall not at any time he narrowed by means of any abutment or structure to the extent of less than twenty feet, nor shall the clear headway from the surface of the highway to the centre be less than fourteen feet, unless otherwise directed or permitted by the board.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Twenty feet would not be wide enough for two lines of tram car track, but I suppose it will be in the discretion of that board to make the width greater ?
You have to leave the power somewhere and cannot provide for every case.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I perhaps did not correctly hear what the minister said. I venture to think that twenty feet is not wide enough. The minister says you cannot make provisions for every case, that subsequent arrangements can be made, and the power must be left somewhere. But I would submit what has been urged upon the minister before, that he should make the prima facie case in favour of the people. The general opening over highways should be wider than twenty feet. People driving have to pass others beneath these railways, and pretty wide loads must pass. Moreover, sometimes, ditches have to be constructed along the abutments to carry water along the highways, and I think the experience in the rural districts is that twenty feet is not sufficient. Then, as to the height, there is a necessity for providing not merely the height at a central point, but from side to side. I know the Minister of Railways, like the rest of us, is endeavouring to protect the public. This Bill is one that probably will not be amended for some time-I venture to say that it will not be amended in favour of the public at any rate. Therefore. I think that it should be made now as favourable to the public as is consistent with justice. A railway company can

easily carry a span of more than twenty feet. They can carry a span of thirty feet to-day more easily than they could one of fifteen feet a few years ago.
How would it do to make the clause read that the opening over a highway should not be less than, thirty or thirty-five feet except with the permission of the board of commissioners '!

I do not think that there is practically any difference. The Bill provides that before these structures can be put up plans and profiles must be submitted to the board. If the company proposed to run a double track they would be required to make a wider structure than for the purposes of a single track, and if running a single track twenty feet would be ample. I do not think we could very well change the section. I have had the opinion of our engineers and have gathered all the information that I could upon the subject, and have reached the conclusion that, so far as the width is concerned, the width that we have named here is all right. In the great majority of cases, a span of twenty feet would be covered by girders. But if you had thirty feet or over, you would compel them ordinarily, to arch, and you would be making a width which, I am assured by competent authorities, is quite unnecessary. This is a limitation upon the board; they are net in any case to allow a width of less than twenty feet; hut they have power to make the width as great as the circumstances of the ease call for. I do not think we can do better than leave the discretion there.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I do not think I have succeeded in making clear to the minister what I have in view. If you make the normal width twenty-five feet, the railway company go on and construct the openings in that way, or else they will make an application to the board. It is a comparatively easy matter for the railway company to appear before the board and they can get an order, perhaps, for all highways along the whole line of a new piece of construction. But it is a serious matter for a municipality to be obliged to initiate these proceedings. Therefore, I think, the minister will see the importance and the justice of making this width ample in the first place, and leaving to the railways, if, in any case it is not necessary to make, the opening so wide, to apply for a modification of the rule. In this case it is a railway carrying a road across the public highway. The people, have prima facie, the first right. That right should be guarded, and then let the railway company show from time to time the necessity for modification. I know this view will commend itself to the minister. He has taken a great deal of trouble to perfect this Bill and it will stand as a monument to him.

I have made inquiries into this matter. If the information I have gained had led me t* believe that a greater width tlfan twenty feet should be placed in this Bill, I should be very glad indeed to amend the Bill and make the width greater than I here propose. But I am advised that twenty feet is ample. How many turnpikes have you in the country with a width exceeding twenty feet ? Very few. I notice also that the bridges which the municipalities are building are not twenty feet wide as a rule. Most of them are sixteen to eighteen feet wide. Why then is it necessary to have a greater width for this class of structure than for the turnpikes or the bridges they carry ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The minister asks, why have the opening under a railway of a greater width than the floor of the bridge. It seems to me the answer is obvious. You must provide width not merely for the wheels which rest upon the roadway, but for the load which often extends far outside the wheels.

There may be some difficulties by making it read ' the centre of the bridge.' I can cite one instance that occurred in my township where a railway crosses a public road where there is not room for a load of hay to go through owing to the way the sides of the crossing are constructed. I think we should require that the crossing should be at least twenty feet square from the bottom to the top and fourteen feet at the top. It should be twenty feet from the bottom and not from the centre.

We are placing upon this independent tribunal the responsibility of requiring plans to be submitted to them and the obligation of seeing that those plans when carried out, should be such as will ensure the public safety. We cannot frame our sections so as to meet every case that may arise, we can only state the maximum and the minimum and leave the rest to the commissioners. We may depend upon them to see that the structures shall be of such a character as will conform with the conditions which we require, that is to say, will ensure safety and protection to the public.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I have not heard yet why the minister changed these words from ' the lowest portion ' to ' the centre.' '
I have not changed them, that is the old Act.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I think the original Bill is better than the old Act. I have not seen any answer why the overhead structure should not be of the same height all the way along, because if it were right to


make it thirteen feet high in the middle, it is equally necessary to make it thirteen feet high all through.

Does the hon. gentleman really see that he is fighting a mere shadow ? Is it to be supposed that this railway commission are going to sanction a structure which will be like the wigwam of an Indian ? The difficulty is this : The old Act used the expression of ' the centre,' the legislators perhaps not knowing the difficulties of the construction. Now it turns out from the experience of the engineers that that term is entirely inappropriate. No matter how wide they required the structure to be, no matter how large the circle was which constituted the arch, there would have to be that fourteen feet below where the arch commences to spring, and it would be difficult to define what the lowest portion was. I thought it was safer to go back to the original Act and let the board of commissioners determine each plan and say whether or not they approve it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: There is not much room for a team of horses and a load of hay to pass through a space twenty feet wide and to have much play, especially if the horses are nervous and are frightened by a passing train. If we are going to pass the section at all we should make it a little more favourable to the people.
I thought the minister had concluded that he would alter the section so as to make it clear fourteen . feet over the highway.
Twenty feet wide and fourteen feet high.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
In the majority of country roads they usually use a straight stringer, in some cases there are iron girders, and in some cases wooden. In only two or three instances have I seen stone arches. But what the minister has already said meets the whole difficulty. The board will have control, and except in isolated instances, the board need not require the railway company to carry out the full height of fourteen feet across a span of twenty feet. But the prima facie duty of the railway company and the prima facie right of the people should be a clear uninterrupted headway above the highway of a full width of twenty feet and of a height of fourteen feet. That is all important and I submit that that right should be guarded. It will occur in so few instances that the companies will be building stone or concrete arches that there will be very few occasions when the alteration will have to be made.
On section 101,

I propose to the committee that we shall re-enact the old section with some Mr. LANCASTER.
little change in it. The more I think about it the better I think the old section was. I beg to move :
That the words ' stretching across, or projecting over ' in the first line be struck out, and that the word ' at ' be substituted in lieu thereof and that on the third, fourth and fifth lines the words ' at such height as to leave sixteen feet from the highway to the lower edge of the sign board1 * be struck out.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Is the section as substituted practically the same as the section in the old Act '!
Yes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Is there any legislation as to what height these boards shall be from the ground ?
No.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I do not object to that. Before we leave this section, I would like to say that there was a section in the old Act-section 189-which provided very stringent penalties for delaying works ordered by the Railway Committee of the Privy Council. We have the board substituted for the railway committee but we have not the penalties re-enacted. Section 189 of the old Act provides that the company incurs a penalty of $50 for each day's delay.
All these penalties are in the new Bill.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I see that section 191 of the new Bill provides a penalty of $40 for neglect to comply with the requirements of this section, but we have not the penalty of $50 a day which is a good thing to hurry the company up.

Section 293 of the new Bill provides :
Every company which shall erect, operate or maintain any bridge, approach, tunnel, viaduct, trestle, or any building, erection or structure, in violation of this Act, or of any order or regulation of the board, shall for each offence incur a penalty of fifty dollars.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: That is another thing. That is where a company violates an order of the board, but that does not say if it does not maintain or construct a work when it is ordered to do so, it will incur this penalty. I 'knew of this section and that is why I have asked the question.
Look at section 294 of the Bill.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
Section 294 says :
Every company, director or officer doing, causing or permitting to be done, any matter, act or thing contrary to the provisions of this or the special Act, or to the orders or directions of the Governor in Council, or of the board or minister made hereunder, or omitting to do any
4717

matter, act or thing required to be done on the part of any such company, director or officer, is liable to any person injured thereby for the full amount of damages sustained by such Act or omission ; and if no other penalty is, in this or the special Act, provided for any such act or omission, is liable, for each offence, to a penalty of not less than twenty dollars, and not more than five thousand dollars, in the discretion of the court before which the same is recoverable.
This is not the same as the old Act. This dees not provide a penalty for each day's delay and it is the delay that makes the trouble. The best way to make them hurry up is to flue them so much a day. The clause says that if there is anything they are required to do, and which they do not do they are liable to a penalty and to pay damages, but in common law they would be liable to pay damages if they did not do their duty even without this provision. If the railway neglects to carry out any order, they ought be under a stringent penalty of so much a day as in the old Act.

We have a great many' more penalties and more provisions in this new Bill than are in the old Act and there is the advantage of having them altogether here.
On section 192.
speakername: The MINISTER OP RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
This section says :
The company shall not erect, place or maintain any lines, wires or poles for telegraphs, telephones, or the conveyance of light, heat, power or electricity, upon or along any highway, square or other public place, except by leave of the board.
I propose to amend that section by adding at the end, the words :
And the consent of the local municipal authorities.
This is in principle the same question we were discussing in regard to highway crossings, although in practice it is of still greater importance. This is a new section which gives the company power to erect poles on any highway or square for a purpose not necessary for the undertaking of a railway company, and it enables the company to do that without the consent of the municipal authorities. The railway lias its own right of way and it can erect poles along its own tracks, and when it conies to a highway crossing they can, under ordinary circumstances, string their wires across without placing a pole on the highway. But in an extreme case where there may be a sharp angle or a high building, surely the municipal authorities would allow them to meet such a case and surely the municipal authorities should have power to do so. This provision allows the railway commission to permit these railway companies to interfere with municipal rights without consulting the municipal authorities at all. I cannot see the necessity for this unless it be that it is intended to hold up the municipalities. A railway company could threaten that unless the municipality gave them rights with reference to the station grounds and other such things, they would go to the railway commission and get permission to do what they liked on the streets of that municipality. This is nothing else than a usurpation of the rights of municipalities, it is a deliberate attempt to deprive the municipalities of the rights they have now.
I believe it is ultra vires of this parliament, but the minister does not agree with me, and whether it is ultra vires or not we should not do it. Even if we have the power we should not attempt to exercise it. Who can best look after the highways in a municipality and declare whether wires for the conveyance of light, heat and power should be erected or not ? Surely it is the municipalities who get their rights from the provincial legislatures. What in the world is this clause wanted here for, except it is to benefit the railways. What right has a railway to go into the light, heat, power business in a municipality without the consent of the municipality. What right has a railway to tear up the squares and public places of a municipality without obtaining the consent of the municipality. I wish the member for Annapolis (Mr. Wade) were in his seat, because a while ago he was sure this section provided for the consent of the municipality, but as he now can see it does not, and I am sure we on this side of the House would have his support in defending the rights of the municipalities. The hon. gentleman referred to subsection (f) but if that subsection is meant to cause us to dream that this is giving the power to the municipality, I cannot help thinking that the wording of it is very imperfect if that is the meaning of it. Subsection (f) says :
(f) The opening up of any street, square, or other public place for the erection of poles, or for carrying wires under ground, shall be subject to the supervision of such person as the municipal council may appoint, and such street, square or other public place shall, without any unnecessary delay, be restored, as far as possible. to its former condition.
That means that if it is opened up by order of the board of commissioners who have sole power to do it by section 192, the work may be carried out under the supervision of an officer appointed by the municipality. But the municipal council has no power to say whether the work shall be done or not. That has been all ordered by the railway commission before the municipality is allowed to come on the scene and supervise the work. It is merely a direction to the municipality as to carrying out something which it cannot stop, and which the board are the only people who can say shall happen or not happen. I do not construe subsection (f) as giving control to the municipal council : and that being so. we are here deliberately, by section 192, taking away from the municipality control of its own highways, and handing that control

over to a railway commission. Therefore, the amendment I move is the only proper thing to make the section not only intra vires, as I think it is not as drawn, but to m'ake it what it should be, even if it were intra vires, so that this work should not be done without the consent of the local authorities.

The hon. member will see that l propose an amendment to this section so that his amendment will not be applicable. I propose to substitute for section 192 the following :
No lines or wires for telegraphs, telephones, or the conveyance of light, heat, power or electricity, shall be erected, placed or maintained across the railway without leave of the board.
I do not say anything about highways there at all. This is a matter relating to railways, and the use of telephone and telegraph lines, and the conducting of electricity in connection with railway undertakings, which are the only things with which we are concerned. Then, I propose the following as subsection 2 of section 192 :
2. Upon any application for such leave, the applicant shall submit to the board a plan and profile of the part of the railway proposed to be affected, showing the proposed location of such lines and wires and the works contemplated in connection therewith ; and the board may grant such application, and may order by whom, hew. when, and on what terms and conditions and under what supervision such works shall be executed ; and upon such order being made such lines and works may be erected, placed and maintained across the railway, subject to and in accordance with such order.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: As I understand, then, this actually prohibits the municipalities-
No, it has nothing to do with municipalities at all. It applies only to a railway line.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Suppose a railway runs through a city, and the city proposes to erect a telephone system crossing that railway. The city could be prevented completing its system unless it got the approval of this board.	[DOT]
Unless it got the board's permission to cross the railway.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I understand that the municipality is to be prevented from carrying out a telephone system or a system of electric lighting, according to its own scheme, unless it gets the approval of a body constituted by this parliament.
Yes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Is not that a most extraordinary thing ?
I think it is a very proper thing. Mr. LANCASTER.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: That would take away the right of the municipality altogether. If the railway is coming in, it ought to be subsidiary to the right of the municipality.

I do not think so. I do not think any electric light or telephone or telegraph company should be allowed to carry its wires across a railway without being subject to the safe and proper running of the railway. There must be some control. That is all that this means, and it could not possibly be permitted to anybody, in the interest of a municipality, which had no concern as to the safe and proper running of trains, to carry a line of electric wires across the railway tracks without permission of the properly constituted authority.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Is it not the duty of this parliament to make the railway provide for public safety in that case ? Why compel the municipalities to do all this ? I would like to record my vote against that clause.
I am sure the hon. gentleman does not understand it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I suppose this lias no retroactive effect and will only apply to railways to be built after this comes into force.
Mr. LANCASTER, I am afraid it will affect railways already in existence.
Of course it will. If a municipality wants to string wires across a railway track, it will have to do so according to the regulations and conditions imposed by the commission.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: In every town and village there are hundreds of wires for telephonic and lighting purposes passing over railways at present.
They will only be allowed subject to conditions imposed by the railway commission just as they are imposed to-day by the Railway Committee of the Privy Council.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
Before we get through with this Bill, it will be found that there will be nothing left for anybody to do but to bow down to the railways, when these railways have the sanction of the commission. I entirely agree with my hon. friend for West Toronto. We do not want a municipality to prevent a railway from running but neither do we want the municipalities to give way to the railways in every thing. The railway need not go into the municipality, and if it does go into a town or village it goes there to make money and should be made subject to the rights of the municipality.

On section 193,
The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS moved that section 193 be amended by striking out the first and second subsections and inserting the following :-
When a company is empowered by a special Act of the parliament of Canada to construct, ooerate and maintain lines of telegraph, telephone or for the convenience of light, heat, power or electricity, the company may, with the consent of the municipal council or other authority having jurisdiction over any highway, square or other public place, enter thereon for the purpose of exercising the said power, and as often as the company think proper may break up or open any highway, square or other public place, subject however to the following provisions :
(a)	The company shall not interfere with the public right of travel.
(b)	Provided that where the company cannot obtain such consent from such municipal council or other authority, the company may apply to the board for leave to exercise such power ; and upon such application shall submit to the board a plan of such highway, square or other public place, showing the proposed location of such lines, wires and poles ; and the board may grant such application in whole or in part and may change or fix the route of such lines, wires or poles, and may by order impose any terms, conditions or limitations in respect thereof that It may deem expedient, having due regard to all proper interests ; and upon such order being made, the company may exercise such powers in accordance with such order and shall, in the performance and execution thereof or in the repairing, renewing or maintaining of such lines, wires or poles, conform to and be subject to the provisions in subsection one of this section provided, as if consent bad been obtained from such ihunlcipal council or other authority, except in so far as the same may be so expressly varied by order of the board.
You will observe that they must first apply to the municipal council for consent, then if the council will not consent, they may appeal to the board. It will not be possible for the company to insist or the council absolutely and arbitrarily to refuse. This tribunal decides between the parties, as any independent tribunal would, as to whether or not this power ought to be given and under what condition.
Do I understand that this clause is intended to reaffirm practically the Act passed twenty years ago ?
This Act as amended was passed in 1899. It is not twenty years old.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I understand there was some litigation arising out of the Act of 1899-out of some defect in the legislation with respect to the Bell Telephone Company's rights.
We have nothing to do with the Bell Telephone Company; we are dealing with railway companies.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
But I am dealing with the rights of municipalities. Do I understand the Minister of Railways to say that
it will rest with the board of commissioners to say whether any railway company whose work has been declared a work for the general advantage of Canada may erect poles on the highways and squares of the city to carry on telephone business, lighting, heating or anything else ? Surely that cannot be the position of the minister.
No. it does not do that.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Then, what does it do ?
The railway company may be authorized, in connection with its own business to have'telephones, electric wires for lighting and so on. But this must be sanctioned by the hoard of commissioners.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Is that perfectly clear ?
It provides that the company may do what they are authorized by its special Act to do. But we restrict that to the exercise of their powers for the purpose of tlie railway and its undertaking.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: But that does not help us very much, whether the special Act restricts or does not restrict. We are providing that the railway commissioners can authorize the railway company to carry on telephones, lighting or heating. Suppose that some future parliament, in its good nature, does not impose such a restriction as the minister has suggested, does that make the legislation any more sensible ?
No, it does not apply to that at all.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
This is the Act we are passing, and now is the time for us to make restrictions that we think should apply. You say the municipalities should give their consent and the minister evidently thinks they will give their consent. But I do not think that anything can be done in control of the streets without the consent of the municipality. And so this law would be not only inadvisable but ultra vires of this legislature. This parliament lias power to give a charter for the carrying out of the undertaking and to do wihat may be necessary for that purpose. But the danger is that more than this will be done without the authority of the municipalities. The streets and highways are vested in the municipal authorities; that is the power that has control of them, and I do not think that this parliament can assist those powers or take them away. But I do not want to make legislation merely trusting to its being held to be ultra vires. I do not think we should authorize the board to undertake to force the municipalities to do with regard to the streets and public places of a municipality what they do not want to do, unless it is absolutely necessary for the purpose of the undertaking which we charter.

And I say that you have only the right to give the power to do what may be necessary to carry out the undertaking. But that cannot he so in the case the hon. minister put.
Do I understand the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lancaster) to say that it is only the question of necessity which confers upon this parliament the right to legislate upon the subject ?
speakername: The MINISTER OB RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: If the hon. gentleman wants to put it that way, I say that it is ultra vires of this parliament to interfere with a municipality except for the carrying out of a purpose for which this parliament has a right to give a charter, and the only reason why railways can force their way across the highways and so on, is because you cannot make the railway otherwise. But where it is not necessary for the purpose of the undertaking to carry poles or wires, this should not be' allowed. The company may carry these things along their own rights of way, but if they1 wish to extend they should buy another right of way. It is surely not right to say that we can authorize a board of commissioners to give a railway company the right to do other than railway business on the streets of a municipality simply because we have the power 'to allow the building of a railway along or across the streets, The railway commission does not care about the municipal rights, but is considering the general interest of Canada, and they might think it in the general interests of Canada to allow railways to run here and there wherever they please. They are not the protectors of the highways, but the municipal authorities are. Recognizing that, this power should be conditional upon the consent of the municipal authorities. Surely this is a case in which the municipal authorities ought to have something to say.

This involves, probably the most serious question we have had to face in connection with this Bill. We are confronted with the proposition of the minister to leave enormous power in the hands of the board. We virtually, as it seems to me, substitute, for what we contemplated before, the right of legislation by this board. The minister shakes his head, meaning, I suppose, that he does not agree with what l have said. We cannot expect the minister always to agree with us; but I can only submit it to his consideration in the hope 'that he may change his mind. The minister has taunted an hon. member on this side with having failed to protest with regard to some matter, I think connected with electric railways. Therefore I wish to state my position as emphatically as I can at this point though I do not know that it will have any effect so far as the minister is concerned. The hon. minister says Mr. LANCASTER.
that this only confers upon the railway company powers in connection with the undertaking of the railway company itself. I should not have so interpreted it.

I say that this proposed legislation does not give a railway company the right to go into the electric light business, or the power business, or the telephone business for any purpose outside of their own undertaking.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Although I have no desire to obstruct this Bill, yet I do submit that it is regretable that large amendments are proposed by the minister, often upon the spur of the moment, when we are not able to understand their effect. These amendments are virtually a recasting the section. I submit that in view of the importance of this legislation, and in order that the company may have an opportunity of judging the effect of these amendments, they should be submitted to us a sufficient time in advance to give us an opportunity of studying them. I confess that I am not sure that I grasp the full scope of the proposed amendment. I believe it is trenching seriously upon the rights of municipalities, and it has this additional bad element, that it transfers tlie matter to a tribunal which should never have the power to legislate for a municipality. If we are to divest ourselves of any power of control over railway companies, let us hand it to the municipalities rather than to this board.

- That amendment will give to the company the power of generating electricity or generating power, and that which they do not use for the purpose of the railway, they can dispose of under their special Act. It gives them the power of going on to the streets of a municipality. If the municipality objects to letting them come upon their streets, then they can apply to the board and the board may give them the right of going anywhere. The clause does not restrict the power to the purpose of the railway company, but it gives them the general power to use these streets for the exercise of the powers they have under their special Act.

Of course, if parliament were to pass an Act giving a railway company the power to run a telegraph business independently and outside the purposes of their undertaking, or an electric light or power business outside of its undertaking, then it would give them an unrestricted power. But parliament is not giving them that power. We have had a great many Acts passed during the present session, and with one exception, I think every railway enterprise going through a section of country where there is a water power upon which they would have to depend for their motive

power to generate electricity was allowed to dispose to the general public of any surplus power they might have over and above what they required for their own purpose. But the railways which have power to erect telegraph and telephone lines and works of that kind, have been strictly limited to the purposes of their undertaking.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: That is for telegraph lines and telephones. But this goes further, and gives a company power to generate electricity for lighting and heating and power purposes, for running factories or anything of that kind. They have that right under their charter, and when I was Minister of Railways and Canals and since then, a good many companies have been given that power, but they have no right to enter upon the streets of any municipality without the consent of the municipality. This gives them the power to go into a municipality and to dispose to the public of a portion of their electricity.

They could carry telegraph lines upon the streets of Toronto. If it is conceded that they have that right, surely the minister ought to make a provision that they should not go and dispose of the extra and unrequired light, heat and power jvithout the consent of the municipality. Is not this the place to make that provision ?
No.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Where is it ?
In the special Act incorporating the company.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Then the contention of my hon. friend from Lanark is admitted by the minister to be correct.

I admit that if parliament does give them the power they could use it, but if they do not get the power, they cannot use it. We have incorporated here provisions which restrict the company as fully as we think it is proper for the company to be restricted. We say they shall procure consent if they can; if they cannot, and if they can make out a case to satisfy the board, then the board may override the decision of the municipal council. The municipal council will not have power absolutely to block an undertaking which has been chartered by this parliament. Then we say that the opening up any streets, square or other public place, is to be subject to the supervision of the municipal council.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
The hon. minister will see, of course, that a company might generate ten times as mpch power as it would require to operate its line of railway. It
might generate ten times as much heat and light as it would require. According to our contention it has no right to tear up the streets, squares and public places of a municipality to dispose of the other nine-tenths that it does not require without the consent of the municipality. It has no right to go into such a business as that. I want to be recorded as very strongly against such a proposition.
Shall clause 193 as amended be adopted ?

I object to it.
Section, as amended, agreed to.
On section 194,
Before section 194 is taken up

I think we had better not enter into any question of drainage to-night. It is too late. I move that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again.
Progress reported.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS moved the adjournment of the House.
Before this motion is adopted, will the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals give us the order of business for tomorrow ?

We will take up the Railway Bill and supply.
Mi-. MONK. What estimates will be taken up ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: We have not yet finished the estimates of the Department of Agriculture.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I understand that the lion. Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. "Mr. Blair) has appointed a special commissioner to make an inquiry into the cause of the accident at West Lome one or two months ago, and that that commissioner has returned to Ottawa after having made an investigation. I would like to ask the hon. minister if the commissioner has submitted his report, and if so, if be will lay it on the Table of the House ?
I have not heard from him for the last two or three days, but when the report is completed I will bring it down.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.
